mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Coastal housing and land reclamation reduce or degrade estuarine habitat. Proposed scope <50% is a preliminary inference from geographically concentrated development, not a population-weighted estimate. Review regional coverage and cumulative habitat loss. Land-use planning and habitat protection are feasible but may conflict with development interests. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.4; SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Port, marina and industrial development can displace dolphins and alter habitat use. Scope <50% requires regional validation. Distinguish habitat alteration here from vessel strikes (4.3) and noise (9.6.3); their impacts must not be added mechanically. Review current projects and mitigation effectiveness. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.4; SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3.

Marine and freshwater aquaculture may release chlorine-based disinfectants, phosphate-containing fertilisers and pharmaceuticals, including antibiotics and antiparasitic agents, into connected coastal habitats. These inputs warrant assessment as potential exposure pathways through water, sediments and prey. The CMP documents bioaccumulation of persistent contaminants, including high organochlorine concentrations in Guiana dolphin tissues, while SALVE recognises chemical pollution among the cumulative threats to the species. However, these assessments do not attribute the reported tissue burdens specifically to aquaculture or demonstrate high tissue concentrations of all the chemical groups listed above. Phosphate enrichment should also be considered through eutrophication and effects on prey availability. Confirm local chemical use, trophic transfer and source attribution before assigning aquaculture-specific scores. Sources: CMP (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.2 and Annex III; Farro et al. (2025), SALVE, doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3. General chemical-use context: FAO, Responsible aquaculture at the production level, https://www.fao.org/4/W4493E/w4493e07.htm.

The chemical-exposure considerations in the comment above also apply where the scale of aquaculture is unknown. Confirm the production system and scale before selecting row 2.4.2 or 2.4.3; do not score the same operation twice.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Review required: the CMP identifies oil and gas activities as a potential source of disturbance and pollution. Confirm current overlap with occupied coastal habitat before assigning scope. Include spills at drilling sites here; assign other spills to 9.2.1 and underwater noise to 9.6.3. No global demographic effect has been quantified. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1 and Annex III.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Mining-related contamination is relevant to some coastal catchments, but exposure pathways and affected population shares require confirmation. Please identify the sites, contaminants and evidence linking extraction or transport to dolphin exposure. Avoid duplicating effluent effects scored under 9.2.2. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.2; SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Possible vessel-strike injuries and overlap with shipping channels support retaining this threat. Diagnostic certainty and collision mortality are incompletely quantified. Scope <50% is a provisional judgment for high-traffic areas. Review necropsy evidence, vessel types and local abundance. Routing and speed management are feasible options. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.3.

level2: 5.4.1 Intentional use: subsistence/small scale (species being assessed is the target)[harvest]
mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Directed capture for bait, consumption or other uses is reported locally. Separate deliberate killing from subsequent use of incidentally caught animals. Scope <50% is provisional; confirm recent occurrence and regional extent. Enforcement and livelihood-sensitive engagement are needed. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.1 and Annex III.

level2: 5.4.3 Unintentional effects: subsistence/small scale (species being assessed is not the target)[harvest]
mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Small-scale gillnet bycatch is a principal documented source of direct mortality. Proposed scope 50-90% is an expert-review hypothesis based on widespread coastal overlap, not a measured population share. Severity remains Unknown because global threat-specific decline is unresolved; this does not indicate low priority. Review regional mortality, abundance and recovery bias. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.1; SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3.

level2: 5.4.4 Unintentional effects: large scale (species being assessed is not the target)[harvest]
mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Incidental capture in industrial fisheries is recognised in the Brazilian assessment. Scope is left open because fleet size and gear deployment are not consistently reported across the range. Classify fisheries using the CSG operational definition, rather than national labels alone. Confirm affected fleets, mortality and separation from row 5.4.3. SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3; CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.1.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Dolphin watching and recreational boating overlap with resident populations. Disturbance is documented in several localities, but demographic effects remain uncertain. Scope <50% is provisional. Please review operator practices, exposure frequency and evidence of displacement; avoid duplicating noise and collision effects. Codes of conduct and enforcement are feasible. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.3.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Proposed placement for named non-viral pathogens where biogeographic origin is unresolved, including Brucella spp., Toxoplasma gondii and Paracoccidioides spp. Confirm taxonomy and the appropriate CSG category. Scope <50% reflects documented local occurrence, with substantial surveillance gaps. Pollution reduction and health surveillance are feasible; population-level control is uncertain. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.5.

mitigation: No, methods do not exist or implementation is needed at a broader scale than the species range.
comment: Cetacean morbillivirus caused major local mortality in Rio de Janeiro; other viral infections are also reported. Ongoing refers to continuing disease risk, not a continuous epizootic. Scope <50% is provisional and surveillance-dependent. Review present circulation and recurrence. Direct population-level mitigation is unproven; surveillance alone does not prevent mortality. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.5; SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Sewage exposes coastal populations to contaminants, nutrients and pathogens. Scope <50% is a provisional estimate for documented affected estuaries. Review wastewater coverage and health evidence. Sanitation improvements can reduce exposure, but implementation across municipalities may require substantial investment. Avoid duplicating pathogen-related mortality. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, sections 6.1.2 and 6.1.5.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Urban runoff is a plausible and documented pollution pathway in developed coastal catchments. Scope <50% requires confirmation from occupied habitats and local source data. Distinguish runoff from sewage and industrial discharge; contaminant detection alone cannot identify the source. Global severity is unresolved. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.2.

REVIEW REQUIRED. Retain oil spills as a candidate threat, but confirm whether relevant exposure is ongoing or future before scoring. Distinguish shipping-related spills from spills at drilling sites (3.1). Provide event dates, affected populations and health or mortality evidence. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, sections 6.1.2 and 6.1.4.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Industrial and mining discharges are plausible sources of metals and persistent contaminants. Scope <50% is provisional and does not establish source attribution. Confirm the fit of this row, whose description also includes industrial facilities. Review toxicological evidence separately from demonstrated demographic effects. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.2.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Organochlorine pesticides are documented in dolphins, but historical residues and ongoing inputs must be distinguished. Ongoing refers to continued exposure to persistent residues. Scope is unresolved. Please identify catchment-specific agricultural sources and temporal trends before finalising this category. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.2.

REVIEW REQUIRED. Garbage and solid waste are a candidate exposure pathway. Please provide species-specific ingestion, entanglement or habitat-impact records, with location and date, before assigning timing or scope. Score abandoned fishing gear consistently with fisheries categories to avoid duplicating mortality. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, section 6.1.2.

mitigation: Yes, methods exist or could be developed in a timely manner to mitigate the threat.
comment: Shipping, dredging and port construction generate underwater noise. Changes in habitat use and acoustic behaviour have been reported, but population-level decline attributable to noise is unresolved. Scope <50% is provisional for documented high-exposure areas. Review sound exposure, duration and mitigation performance. CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, sections 6.1.2 and 6.1.4; SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3.

mitigation: No, methods do not exist or implementation is needed at a broader scale than the species range.
comment: Future habitat alteration is a proposed assessment of climate-related risk. Scope remains unresolved because range-wide exposure cannot be equated with adverse population effects. Please supply species-specific projections, their time horizons and uncertainty. Local adaptation may reduce vulnerability, while control of the climatic driver requires broader action. SALVE: Farro et al. (2025), doi:10.37002/salve.ficha.14515.3; CMP: Governments of Brazil, Costa Rica, France & Panama (2024), SC/69B/CMP/18 rev1, Annex III, climate-change discussion.
